nameStory: Araneus bivittatus gets its scientific name from the Latin 'bivittatus,' meaning 'with two stripes' or 'two-banded.' This likely refers to distinctive markings or patterns on the spider's body that help distinguish it from its many orbweaver cousins. The name hints at the key feature early spider scientists noticed when first describing this species.
description: The Araneus bivittatus is a medium-sized orbweaver spider that builds the classic circular webs we often associate with spiders. Like other members of the Araneus genus, it has a rounded, somewhat bulbous abdomen and relatively thick legs compared to some other web-building spiders. These spiders are part of the largest orbweaver family, known for their engineering prowess in creating those perfect spiral webs. While not as commonly encountered as some of its relatives, it shares the typical orbweaver body plan with a compact, sturdy build.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for distinctive striped or banded patterns on the abdomen that give this spider its 'two-striped' name, though individual variation can make this subtle

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds classic circular orb webs with sticky spiral threads that feel tacky to the touch if accidentally encountered

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Has the typical orbweaver build with a rounded, bulbous abdomen that feels firm if gently touched, and sturdy legs

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized for an orbweaver, with the body spanning roughly the size of a large pea when legs are excluded

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits in the center of its web or hides nearby, quickly rushing out when prey vibrates the web strands

habitat: This orbweaver can be found in various habitats throughout New England, typically in areas with vegetation that provides good anchor points for web construction. Look for them in gardens, forest edges, and areas with shrubs or tall plants where they can string their webs between branches. They prefer spots with some protection from strong winds but enough open space to catch flying insects.

seasonality.spring: Adults may be active in late spring, beginning to establish territories and build webs as insect prey becomes more abundant.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, building and maintaining webs, mating, and the females preparing egg sacs.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity continues into early fall, with females focusing on egg-laying before cooler weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, with the species overwintering as eggs or young spiders in protected locations.

funFact: Despite being relatively uncommon with only 9 recorded observations in New England, this spider belongs to one of the most diverse spider genera in North America, with nearly 20 different Araneus species calling New England home!
confusionNotes: With so many Araneus relatives in New England, identifying this species can be tricky without close examination of the markings. Focus on the banded or striped pattern suggested by its name, and remember that many orbweavers look similar from a distance. When in doubt, note the web location and take photos of the abdomen pattern for later identification.
contextualKnowledge: The genus Araneus represents one of the most successful groups of web-building spiders, with species found across the globe. This particular species highlights how even within a single genus, there can be both common species like the Cross Orbweaver and rarer finds like A. bivittatus sharing the same general habitat.
compareHints: Among its Araneus relatives, A. bivittatus can be distinguished by its specific striped pattern, setting it apart from the cross-shaped markings of the Cross Orbweaver or the marbled patterns of the Marbled Orbweaver. It lacks the distinctive shamrock-shaped marking of the Shamrock Orbweaver and the prominent white spots of some other relatives. The key is looking for those characteristic bands or stripes that give it its two-striped name.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the Marbled Orbweaver which has swirled, mottled patterns, the Cross Orbweaver's white cross marking is clean and distinct.

Among New England's Araneus orbweavers, the marbled orbweaver is unique for its extremely inflated, almost spherical abdomen—much rounder than the Cross Orbweaver's more egg-shaped belly or the Shamrock Orbweaver's triangular markings.

Among its Araneus cousins, the barn orbweaver is distinguished by its strong preference for wooden human structures, while the cross orbweaver favors gardens and the marbled orbweaver prefers trees and shrubs.

Among its Araneus cousins, the shamrock orbweaver's white spots make it relatively easy to distinguish - the cross orbweaver has a distinctive white cross pattern, while the marbled orbweaver shows complex marbled coloring without distinct dots.

Nordmann's Orbweaver is generally less distinctively marked than its famous cousins like the Cross Orbweaver (which has a prominent white cross pattern) or the Marbled Orbweaver (with its striking yellow and black marbled appearance).

Among the Araneus orbweavers, the Giant Lichen Orbweaver stands out for its specific lichen-mimicking camouflage, while relatives like the Cross Orbweaver have distinct white cross markings and the Marbled Orbweaver displays smooth, flowing color patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Fierce Orbweaver stands out for its bold behavioral responses rather than distinctive markings like the Cross Orbweaver's white cross or the Marbled Orbweaver's marbled patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Lattice Orbweaver's crosshatch pattern sets it apart from the distinctive white cross of the Cross Orbweaver and the swirled, marble-like patterns of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Unlike the Cross Orbweaver which prefers gardens and woodland edges, or the Marbled Orbweaver found on trees, the Openfield Orbweaver specifically chooses exposed grasslands and meadows.

Among its Araneus relatives in New England, the Red-spotted Orbweaver is most easily distinguished by its reddish markings - the Cross Orbweaver has a white cross pattern, the Marbled Orbweaver has marbled yellow and brown coloring, and the Shamrock Orbweaver has a distinctive shamrock-like pattern.

Among the many Araneus orbweavers in New England, the Butterfly Orbweaver stands out for its wing-like geometric patterns rather than the cross-shaped markings of the Cross Orbweaver or the marble-stone appearance of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Among its many Araneus relatives in New England, the Juniper Orbweaver's defining characteristic is its habitat specialization rather than distinctive markings.

Unlike the Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross pattern on the back, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its orange and white marbled appearance, the White-bellied Orbweaver's key feature is underneath rather than on top.

Among its Araneus cousins in New England, the Red-backed Orbweaver's bright green front section makes it stand out from the typically brown or gray Cross Orbweaver and the yellow-and-black patterned Marbled Orbweaver.
Distinguishing Araneus iviei from its many orbweaver relatives in New England requires expert knowledge, as most species in this genus share similar web-building behavior and general body structure.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its mottled, marbled pattern, the Black-spotted Orbweaver displays clear black spots as its defining feature.

Unlike the abundant Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the variable Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, Araneus bonsallae lacks well-documented field marks for New England populations.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its white cross markings or the Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, the Humped bog orbweaver's most distinctive feature is its physical shape rather than its coloration.
